newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COCOA--Brazil's Ceplac denies closure rumours.
newsitem.headline: COCOA--Brazil's Ceplac denies closure rumours.

text.p: Brazil's cocoa institute Ceplac denied rumours that it could be dismantled as part of government spending cuts.
"Talk about getting rid of Ceplac is just speculation," said Carlos Fernando Brito, director of the institute's office in Salvador, the capital of the cocoa-producing state of Bahia.
Brito said Ceplac played a crucial role in the region, especially in the fight against witch's broom disease which has decimated production in the area in the last five years.

He said the institute was carrying out research into finding more resistant varieties of cocoa trees and into finding pesticides which could provide effective protection against the disease, which at present has no known cure.
Ceplac employs a total of 3,000 people in the states of Bahia, Espirito Santo, Amazonas and Para, although the majority are based at a site near the city of Itabuna in the heart of the cocoa region.
These included 100 fully qualified researchers. "We have a top team of researchers and it would be a serious blow for the region if Ceplac was to be de-activated," he said.

He said Ceplac also ran educational programmes for farmers, mainly on crop husbandry and ways of fighting witch's broom and podrot. A large majority of Brazilian public employees were given job stability by the 1988 constitution and are almost impossible to sack.
Brito said that one of the major worries of the government's reform package was that 41 of Ceplac's scientists are not protected and could therefore face the axe.
However, most of the other employees have stability and if the government did extinguish Ceplac, it would simply have to deploy them elsewhere making the exercise fairly pointless.

Ceplac has been criticised as being ineffective by some cocoa traders but Brito said the problem had been caused by the failure of the government to pass on all the money which had been allocated to it.
This year, the government budgeted $17 million Real for Ceplac, which Brito said is enough for the needs of the institute, but some of this was withheld.
"Ceplac is recognised as being the most efficient organisation in the Ministry of Agriculture," he said.
"But this year we didn't get all the resources we need. We have around 50 offices around the region and they money to be able to buy fuel to get to the farms. If they can't buy it, they can't work."
